```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# The ragg device writes smaller figure files; without it the default is used.
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = digits), "%")
```

This vignette is a case study of a small meta-analysis. A meta-analysis
often has only a dozen or two studies, which is not many for a model
that estimates the whole distribution of effects. We fit the model to 19
studies, and then use fits on other ranges of the grid and a simulation
study to see how much of the result comes from the data.

```{r library}
library(bayesEfron)
```

We use the 19 studies of teacher expectancy that @raudenbush1985
analyzed. In these experiments, teachers were led to expect unusual
intellectual growth from pupils who had in fact been chosen at random.

## The teacher expectancy studies

The data frame `raudenbush1985` has one row for each study:

```{r data}
head(raudenbush1985[, c("study", "author", "year", "weeks", "yi", "sei")])
```

`yi` is the standardized mean difference in IQ between the pupils the
teachers expected more from and the others, and `sei` is its standard
error. `weeks` is the number of weeks that the teachers had known their
pupils before the expectancy was induced. @raudenbush1984 related the
size of the effect to this prior contact. See `?raudenbush1985` for the
sources.

```{r data-facts, include = FALSE}
studies <- raudenbush1985
recent <- studies$weeks <= 1
by_se <- rank(-studies$sei)
top <- order(studies$yi, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
stopifnot(nrow(studies) == 19L, sum(recent) == 8L,
          mean(studies$yi[recent]) > 0.4, mean(studies$yi[!recent]) < 0,
          identical(sort(top), c(4L, 10L, 11L)), all(studies$yi[top] > 0.5),
          sum(studies$yi > 0.5) == 3L,
          # The three largest estimates are in the less precise half.
          all(by_se[top] <= 9), by_se[4] == 1)
print(c(mean(studies$yi[recent]), mean(studies$yi[!recent])))
```

The `r sum(recent)` studies with at most 1 week of prior contact have a
mean estimate of `r num(mean(studies$yi[recent]))`, whereas the other
`r sum(!recent)` have a mean of `r num(mean(studies$yi[!recent]))`. We
do not use `weeks` in the model below. The model treats the 19 effects
as draws from one distribution $g$, so it describes the spread of the
effects without explaining it.

## Fitting and checking the model

bayesEfron gives $g$ no parametric form. It places $g$ on a grid of
equally spaced values, with a probability at each value, and estimates
those probabilities from the data. See `vignette("bayesEfron")` for an
introduction. The grid has to begin and end somewhere, and no effect can
lie outside it.

We fit the model with the default settings:

```{r fit-call, eval = FALSE}
fit <- bayes_efron_fit(raudenbush1985, seed = 1985)
```

The result of this call is in the package as `raudenbush_fit`, thinned
to 1 draw in 15. We load it instead of running the sampler, and check it
with `diagnose()`.

```{r stored-fit}
fit <- raudenbush_fit
diagnose(fit)
```

```{r fit-facts, include = FALSE}
fit <- raudenbush_fit
g_ci <- confint(fit, type = "g")
rownames(g_ci) <- g_ci$parameter
ends <- diagnose(fit)$grid$ends
width <- diff(range(studies$yi))
stopifnot(all(ends$set_by == "estimates"),
          abs(ends$value[1] - (min(studies$yi) - 0.5 * width)) < 1e-8,
          abs(ends$value[2] - (max(studies$yi) + 0.5 * width)) < 1e-8,
          length(diagnose(fit)$sampler_diagnostics_failed) == 0L,
          length(diagnose(fit)$sampler_diagnostics_warned) == 0L,
          g_ci["mean_g", "lower"] < 0, g_ci["sd_g", "lower"] > 0.1)
```

In this output a site is a study. `diagnose()` reports no failed check
and no warning for the run, and `vignette("diagnostics")` explains what
each line means. By default the grid covers the range of the estimates
extended by half its width on each side, unless a short preliminary fit
narrows it. For these data it is not narrowed and runs from
`r num(ends$value[1])` to `r num(ends$value[2])`, as the two `end` lines
show.

## Two estimates of the spread

We plot the estimate of $g$ and its 90% band with `plot_g()`. Setting
`observed = "rug"` marks the 19 estimates on the axis, and
`normal = TRUE` adds, as a dashed curve, the usual normal random-effects
model fitted to the same estimates by restricted maximum likelihood
(REML).

```{r g-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "The estimated density of the 19 effects with a wide band and a long right tail, a narrower dashed normal curve, and marks for the estimates, three of which lie above 0.5."}
plot_g(fit, observed = "rug", normal = TRUE)
```

```{r normal-facts, include = FALSE}
# The normal curve that plot_g() draws, fitted by REML: its mean and its
# standard deviation, from the curve.
curve <- ggplot2::layer_data(plot_g(fit, normal = TRUE), 2L)
curve <- curve[curve$linetype == "dashed", ]
reml_mean <- sum(curve$x * curve$y) / sum(curve$y)
reml_sd <- sqrt(sum((curve$x - reml_mean)^2 * curve$y) / sum(curve$y))
sims <- utils::read.csv(system.file("verification", "few-studies.csv",
                                    package = "bayesEfron"), check.names = FALSE)
tail_own <- g_summary(fit, type = "prob", lower = 0.5)
tail_normal <- 1 - pnorm(0.5, reml_mean, reml_sd)
stopifnot(abs(reml_sd - sims$observed_reml_sd[1]) < 0.002,
          abs(g_ci["sd_g", "mean"] - sims$observed_own_sd[1]) < 1e-6,
          g_ci["sd_g", "mean"] > 2 * reml_sd, reml_sd > g_ci["sd_g", "lower"],
          tail_own$mean > 0.05, tail_normal < 0.005)
print(c(reml_mean, reml_sd, tail_own$mean, tail_own$lower, tail_own$upper, tail_normal))
```

Three of the estimates are above 0.5, from studies 4, 10 and 11, and all
three studies are in the less precise half. Next we print the posterior
summaries of $g$ with `confint()`:

```{r fit}
confint(fit, type = "g")
```

According to the fit, the standard deviation of $g$ is
`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "mean"])` (90% interval
`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "lower"])` to `r num(g_ci["sd_g", "upper"])`) and
its mean is `r num(g_ci["mean_g", "mean"])`
(`r num(g_ci["mean_g", "lower"])` to `r num(g_ci["mean_g", "upper"])`).
The normal model has a mean of `r num(reml_mean)` and a standard
deviation of `r num(reml_sd)`, less than half as large. The two estimates
agree about where most of the effects are but differ in the right tail.
In the bayesEfron estimate `r pct(tail_own$mean, 1)` of the
effects are above 0.5 (90% interval `r pct(tail_own$lower, 1)` to
`r pct(tail_own$upper)`), compared with `r pct(tail_normal, 1)` under
the normal curve.

So the three large estimates can be read in two ways, one for each
curve: as a tail of large effects, or as small effects with large
sampling errors. With 19 studies we can't tell which is right.

## The study with the largest estimate

Study 4 has the largest estimate, `r num(max(studies$yi))`, and the
largest standard error. We plot the posterior distribution of its effect
with `plot_site_posterior()`:

```{r study4-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "For study 4: its posterior density, spread from about 0 to the upper end of the grid with a peak near 0.2, the likelihood of its estimate centered at 1.18, and the estimate of the distribution of effects, peaked near zero."}
plot_site_posterior(fit, sites = 4)
```

Its posterior distribution has a peak near the center of $g$ and a long
shoulder that extends past the estimate to the upper limit of the grid.
We summarize it with `site_summary()` and two calls to
`exceedance_prob()`:

```{r study4}
site_summary(fit, sites = 4)[, c("label", "estimate", "se", "mean", "lower",
                                 "upper")]
exceedance_prob(fit, threshold = 0.3, direction = "below", sites = 4)
exceedance_prob(fit, threshold = 0.8, sites = 4)
```

```{r study4-facts, include = FALSE}
four <- site_summary(fit, sites = 4)
small <- unname(exceedance_prob(fit, 0.3, direction = "below", sites = 4))
large <- unname(exceedance_prob(fit, 0.8, sites = 4))
middle <- 1 - small - large
weight <- reml_sd^2 / (reml_sd^2 + four$se^2)
normal_four <- reml_mean + weight * (four$estimate - reml_mean)
stopifnot(four$estimate == max(studies$yi), four$se == max(studies$sei),
          min(small, middle, large) > 0.3, max(small, middle, large) < 0.37,
          four$upper - four$lower > 1.2, four$lower > 0, four$lower < 0.05,
          normal_four < 0.3, four$mean > 2 * normal_four)
print(c(four$mean, four$lower, four$upper, small, middle, large, normal_four))
```

About a third of the probability is in each of three regions: the effect
is below 0.3 with probability `r num(small)`, between 0.3 and 0.8 with
probability `r num(middle)`, and above 0.8 with probability
`r num(large)`. A distribution of this shape is better summarized by its
90% interval, `r num(four$lower)` to `r num(four$upper)`, than by the
posterior mean of `r num(four$mean)`. We can say that the effect is
probably positive, and not much more. By contrast, the normal model has
no long tail, and it shrinks the same estimate to `r num(normal_four)`.

## Sensitivity to the range of the grid

No effect can lie beyond the limits of the grid, and with few studies
the data carry little information about the part of the range that has
no estimates, so the range is a choice that the results may depend on.
`compare_efron_grids()` fits the model on several ranges. In the call
below we extend the range of the estimates on each side by 0.25, 0.5
(the default) and 1 times its width, and ask for the posterior means of
studies 4 and 8.

```{r comparison-call, eval = FALSE}
comparison <- compare_efron_grids(raudenbush1985, L = 101, M = 6,
                                  expansion = c(0.25, 0.5, 1),
                                  sites = c(4, 8), seed = 1985)
```

Its result also comes with the package, and we read and plot it:

```{r comparison, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "Three rows, one for each range of the grid, with the estimated density, the mean and the standard deviation of the distribution of effects, and the posterior means and intervals of studies 4 and 8. The point for study 4 moves left as the range widens."}
comparison <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "raudenbush_ranges.rds",
                                  package = "bayesEfron"))
plot(comparison)
```

```{r comparison-facts, include = FALSE}
ranges <- as.data.frame(comparison)[order(comparison$expansion), ]
stopifnot(nrow(ranges) == 3L, all(diff(ranges$site_4) < 0),
          max(ranges$site_4) - min(ranges$site_4) > 0.3,
          diff(range(ranges$sd_g)) < 0.03, diff(range(ranges$mean_g)) < 0.03,
          diff(range(ranges$site_8)) < 0.03,
          ranges$divergences[1] > 0, ranges$end_mass[1] > 0.05,
          all(abs(ranges$elpd_diff) <= 2 * pmax(ranges$se_diff, 1e-12)))
# The probability that the estimate of g puts above 0.8 on each range.
above <- vapply(attr(comparison, "g")[as.character(ranges$spec)], function(x) {
  sum(x$mean[x$value > 0.8]) * diff(x$value[1:2])
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(diff(above) < 0), above[1] > 3 * above[3])
# With the 101 points that the call fixes, the widest range is a little
# coarser than the rule for the resolution of a grid asks for.
widest <- suppressWarnings(make_efron_grid(
  raudenbush1985, grid_method = "paper_realdata", expansion = 1, L = 101, M = 6
))$resolution
stopifnot(identical(ranges$adequate, c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)),
          widest$scale_over_spacing > 3.5, widest$scale_over_spacing < 4)
print(ranges[, c("expansion", "lower", "upper", "mean_g", "sd_g", "site_4", "site_8")])
print(above); print(widest$scale_over_spacing)
```

Each row is one range. Across the three ranges the mean and the standard
deviation of $g$ change little, and the standard deviation stays between
`r num(min(ranges$sd_g))` and `r num(max(ranges$sd_g))`. Study 8, which
has the smallest estimate, does not move much either. However, the
posterior mean of study 4 falls from `r num(ranges$site_4[1])` on the
narrowest range to `r num(ranges$site_4[2])` on the default and
`r num(ranges$site_4[3])` on the widest. The reason is in the right tail
of $g$. As the range widens, the estimated probability of an effect
above 0.8 falls from `r pct(above[1], 1)` to `r pct(above[2], 1)` and
then to `r pct(above[3], 1)`.

Printing the comparison shows the checks for each fit:

```{r comparison-table}
comparison
```

The notes under the table flag its second row, the narrowest range. One
study there has more than 5% of its posterior probability in the outer
2% of the grid, at the upper end, and the run has divergent transitions,
so we set this range aside (`vignette("diagnostics")` describes both
checks). The widest range has a smaller problem. With the 101 grid points
that the call fixes, its grid is a little coarser than the package
recommends (`adequate` is `FALSE`): a rough estimate of the spread of
the effects is `r num(widest$scale_over_spacing, 1)` grid spacings, and
at least 4 are recommended. As the last note reports, leave-one-out
cross-validation does not separate the three ranges. See
`vignette("choosing-a-grid")` for how to read such a comparison.

Between the default and the widest range, nothing in the data lets us
decide which posterior mean is right. A report on study 4 should
therefore state the range of the grid together with the posterior mean.

## A simulation with 19 studies

To see what the two analyses make of 19 studies when the truth is known,
we simulated data sets with the 19 standard errors of these studies and
true effects from one of three distributions:

- a normal distribution with the standard deviation that REML estimates,
  `r num(reml_sd)`;
- a normal distribution with the larger standard deviation that
  bayesEfron estimates, `r num(g_ci["sd_g", "mean"])`;
- the posterior mean of $g$ itself, with its right tail (the probability
  of each grid point was spread evenly over its cell).

We fitted each of 200 data sets for each distribution with the defaults
of `bayes_efron_fit()` and with the normal model, holding its mean and
standard deviation at their REML estimates (a plug-in analysis). The
rows labeled `known g` in the table below use the distribution that the
effects were drawn from, which no analysis of real data can do. The
table comes with the package. We leave out its rows for a second
bayesEfron fit, with `adapt_delta = 0.99`, until later.

```{r simulation}
sims <- read.csv(system.file("verification", "few-studies.csv",
                             package = "bayesEfron"), check.names = FALSE)
shown <- sims[sims$method != "bayesEfron, adapt_delta = 0.99", ]
data.frame(effects = shown$scenario, analysis = shown$method,
           true_sd = round(shown$true_sd, 2), sd = round(shown$sd_mean, 2),
           sd_inclusion = shown$sd_inclusion,
           inclusion = round(shown$inclusion, 3),
           length = round(shown$length, 2),
           largest_inclusion = round(shown$largest_inclusion, 3),
           largest_error = round(shown$largest_error, 2))
```

```{r simulation-facts, include = FALSE}
cell <- function(method, column) {
  rows <- sims[sims$method == method, ]
  stopifnot(identical(rows$scenario, c("normal, SD 0.14", "normal, SD 0.31", "fitted g")))
  rows[[column]]
}
own <- function(column) cell("bayesEfron", column)
normal <- function(column) cell("normal", column)
known <- function(column) cell("known g", column)
smaller_steps <- function(column) cell("bayesEfron, adapt_delta = 0.99", column)
truth <- own("true_sd")
longer <- own("length") / known("length") - 1
factor <- own("sd_mean") / normal("sd_mean")
stopifnot(
  all(sims$replications == 200),
  # The bayesEfron intervals have coverage close to 0.90; those of the
  # normal model at its REML estimates do not.
  all(abs(own("inclusion") - 0.9) < 2 * own("inclusion_se")),
  all(own("inclusion_se") < 0.007),
  all(normal("inclusion") < 0.89), normal("inclusion")[1] < 0.75,
  all(longer > 0.05), all(longer < 0.3),
  normal("sd_zero")[1] > 0.09, normal("sd_zero")[1] < 0.12,
  # The standard deviation of g runs high.
  all(own("sd_mean") > 1.2 * truth), all(own("sd_inclusion") < 0.86),
  all(factor > 1.3), factor[1] < 2,
  all(own("both_as_observed") == 0),
  own("own_as_large")[1] < 0.2, own("reml_as_small")[2] == 0,
  # The study with the largest estimate.
  all(abs(own("largest_inclusion") - 0.9) < 0.011),
  all(normal("largest_inclusion") < 0.86),
  all(round(own("largest_error")[1:2], 2) == 0.07), abs(own("largest_error")[3]) < 0.03,
  all(abs(normal("largest_error")[1:2]) < 0.01), normal("largest_error")[3] < -0.1,
  # Divergent transitions, and what smaller steps change.
  all(own("with_divergences") >= 70),
  all(smaller_steps("with_divergences") < 0.4 * own("with_divergences")),
  all(smaller_steps("with_divergences") > 0.3 * own("with_divergences")),
  all(abs(smaller_steps("inclusion_change")) < 0.0015),
  all(abs(smaller_steps("sd_change")) < 0.0015),
  all(abs(own("inclusion_with_divergences") - 0.9) < 0.005),
  all(abs(own("inclusion_with_divergences") - own("inclusion_without_divergences")) < 0.012),
  all(own("end_warnings") == 0),
  sum(diagnose(fit)$divergences) == 0
)
series <- function(x, f = num, ...) {
  x <- trimws(f(x, ...))
  paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), " and ", x[length(x)])
}
print(rbind(truth = truth, own_sd = own("sd_mean"), factor = factor, longer = longer))
```

The columns are:

- `true_sd` and `sd`: the standard deviation of the distribution, and
  the mean of its estimates. The estimate is the posterior mean of the
  standard deviation of $g$ or the REML estimate.
- `sd_inclusion`: for bayesEfron, the proportion of data sets in which
  the 90% interval for that standard deviation contains the true value.
- `inclusion`: the proportion of the true effects inside the studies'
  90% intervals, averaged over the data sets. We call this the coverage
  of the intervals.
- `length`: the mean length of those intervals.
- `largest_inclusion` and `largest_error`: for the study with the
  largest estimate in each data set, the proportion of data sets in
  which its interval contains its true effect, and the mean of its
  posterior mean minus its true effect.

Under all three distributions the bayesEfron intervals have coverage
close to 0.90 (the Monte Carlo standard errors are about 0.006).
However, they pay for it in length, and are `r series(longer, pct)`
longer than the intervals from the known distribution. The normal
model's plug-in intervals cover `r series(normal("inclusion"), pct)` of
the true effects, because they treat two estimated numbers as known.
In `r pct(normal("sd_zero")[1], 1)` of the data sets from the first
distribution, REML estimates the standard deviation as zero, and every
interval is a point.

The standard deviation of $g$ is estimated too large under all three
distributions, and its 90% interval contains the true value in fewer
than 90% of the data sets. The likely cause is the prior distribution,
which favors a $g$ spread over the range, but we have not isolated it.

For the real data this has one consequence above all. Under each of the
three
distributions the bayesEfron estimate exceeds the REML estimate on
average, by factors of `r series(factor, num, 1)`. So a gap between the
two estimates is not by itself evidence of a tail: data of this size
produced one under every distribution that we tried. But the simulation
does not account for all of the gap in the real data. The pair seen
there, a posterior mean of at least `r num(sims$observed_own_sd[1])`
with a REML estimate of at most `r num(sims$observed_reml_sd[1])`,
occurred in none of the 600 data sets. One thing that the simulation
leaves out is a relation between a study's effect and its precision.
Both models assume that there is none, and prior contact may produce one
here. This is a conjecture that we have not tested.

For the study with the largest estimate, each analysis does well when
the true distribution looks like its own estimate of $g$. Under both
normal
distributions the bayesEfron posterior mean is too high by
`r num(own("largest_error")[1])` on average, and the normal model's is
nearly unbiased. Under the fitted $g$ the normal model is too low by
`r num(-normal("largest_error")[3])`, and bayesEfron is nearly unbiased.
We cannot tell from the data which case we are in. The intervals for
that study behave differently. Under all three distributions the
bayesEfron interval contains the true effect in about 90% of the data
sets (a proportion from 200 data sets has a Monte Carlo standard error
of about 2 percentage points), whereas the normal model's interval
contains it in `r series(normal("largest_inclusion"), pct, 1)`.

Finally, the stored fit has no divergent transitions, but of the 200
default fits for each distribution,
`r series(own("with_divergences"), format)` had at least one. With
`adapt_delta = 0.99` the counts were
`r series(smaller_steps("with_divergences"), format)`, and the summaries
did not change, with coverage moving by about 0.001 at most. Among the
default fits, those with divergent transitions also had the same
coverage as the others, to within 0.011. Note that these are averages
over data sets, and not evidence that the warning can be ignored in a
given fit.

## Recommendations for a meta-analysis of this size

Our simulation is limited to one set of 19 standard errors, three
distributions, normal noise, and effects unrelated to precision. Within
those limits, this is what we recommend for 19 studies like these.

- Start with `adapt_delta = 0.99`, which cut the number of fits with
  divergent transitions by about two thirds without changing the
  results.
- Report the intervals of the studies and not only their posterior
  means. The intervals had coverage close to 0.90 under every
  distribution that we tried, whereas the posterior mean of the study
  with the largest estimate was too high under two of them.
- For such a study, fit a narrower and a wider range with
  `compare_efron_grids()` and report the range together with the
  posterior mean.
- Report the standard deviation of $g$ with its interval, and say that
  with so few studies the estimate tends to be too high.
- Do not present the shape of the estimated $g$ as a finding. The band
  in the first plot is wide, and the same model overstates the spread of
  a normal distribution.

The normal model is simpler, but that doesn't make it the safer choice.
Its plug-in intervals contained too few of the true effects under all
three distributions, most of all for the study with the largest estimate.
We have not made the
comparison with a normal model that accounts for the uncertainty in its
variance, as a fully Bayesian one does.

`raudenbush_fit` has only 800 of the 12,000 draws of its run. For a
report, run the `bayes_efron_fit()` call above yourself, with
`adapt_delta = 0.99` added. A fit that you run stores every draw.

## References
